newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Relief for American-Russian space crew delayed.
newsitem.headline: Relief for American-Russian space crew delayed.

text.p: Stuck in space with toilets close to overflowing, the three-man Russian-American crew of the Mir space station suffered another blow when they learned that the arrival of their relief crew had been postponed.

Itar-Tass news agency quoted officials at mission control outside Moscow on Thursday as saying the launch of the replacement team, two Russians and a German, had been put back to February from December 15.
The postponement was caused by financial problems which had delayed production of the Soyuz booster rockets needed for such launches, meaning none was available, it said.
U.S. astronaut John Blaha and his two Russian colleagues, Valery Korzun and Alexander Koleri, have been on board the 10-year-old Mir since September 19.

The three were already grappling with a potentially messy problem concerning disposal of bodily waste fluids. Interfax news agency said a device which recycles the crew's waste into the craft's cooling system had broken down and all the reserve containers were nearly full.
Replacements were not due for weeks and the crew could also not find the pump used to transfer the waste into the cooling system, the agency quoted an unidentified source as saying.

New waste containers were to have been shipped out in October but the supply ship, which was also to bring food, water and fuel to Mir, had been postponed because of the cash crisis. It was now due to be launched only on November 20.
Russian space officials could not be reached for comment.
It will not be the first time cosmonauts and astronauts have had to extend their stay on Mir.

The last crew, which included U.S. astronaut Shannon Lucid, stayed longer than planned, partly because of rocket problems. Lucid set endurance records for both Americans and women in space. Another crew, which left Mir last February, had been forced to stay aboard an extra 52 days.
The problems are the latest to hit Russia's space programme since the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.

Space agency officials have said their funding is down to about a fifth of Cold War levels. Tass said financial problems had meant a 10-fold cutback in production of Soyuz booster rockets compared with the 1980s.
The Baikonur cosmodrome, from where cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin blasted off in 1961 to become the first man in space, has been deprived of much of its funding.
Moscow has to find $115 million a year rent for the base, in the now independent state of Kazakhstan.
On a brighter note, Tass said in a separate report that a Proton booster due to deliver an international space probe to Mars was expected to blast off as scheduled on November 16.

The Mars probe, which Tass said had funding from 22 countries, will deploy two drilling devices to collect data from the planet. The project has been revived after the cash crisis forced its postponement in 1994.
The relief crew for Mir comprises German astronaut Reinhold Ewald and Russians Alexander Lazutkin and Vasily Tsibliyev.
"Ewald will not yet achieve his dream of celebrating Christmas and New Year in space," Tass said.
